idiom_name: interface contract plus a sealed facade class (or readonly struct) holding the implementation
implementation_notes: C# dispatches through interfaces and abstract classes natively, so the envelope degenerates into an ordinary class - or a readonly struct when value semantics matter - with an ILetter field: the interface declares the contract, any number of classes and structs implement it, and explicit interface implementations keep the public surface narrow. When the letter has to be generated rather than written (transparent logging, retry, pooling), System.Reflection.DispatchProxy creates a proxy type that implements the interface and routes every call into a handler. The C++ original's compile-firewall motivation does not exist here (no headers), and objects have reference semantics, so a separate facade type is worth it only for a narrower API, value-like copying or a place for caching and lazy creation.
pitfalls: Classes have reference semantics, so 'copying' an envelope by assignment aliases the same letter; only an explicit Clone() (or a readonly struct holding the letter) gives the value behaviour the pattern promises.
Adding a member to ILetter breaks every hand-written implementor unless it is a default interface member, and a default member silently gives old implementations behaviour nobody wrote for them.
A DispatchProxy-generated letter cannot touch non-public interface members, requires the interface to be public or internal-visible, and pays reflection cost and boxing on every call.
